agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix f2c46512ec48 on top of intro c002e9bc863c via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (UseAfterFree): The prepareForSwap function only copies dynamic element buffers when the buffer is inside the nursery (ChunkPtrIsInsideNursery), but fails to consider the case where a tenured object with a buffer marked as nursery-owned is swapped with a nursery object. When swapping a nursery object with a tenured object, the tenured object can end up with a pointer to a buffer that is marked as nursery-owned. During the next nursery collection, this buffer will be freed because the GC believes it belongs to the nursery, causing a use-after-free when the tenured object later accesses the freed buffer. Root cause: The introduction of the buffer allocator for JSObject elements changed how dynamic element buffers are managed during object swaps. The new code only copies buffers when they are physically inside the nursery memory region, but fails to consider cases where a buffer is allocated via AllocBuffer with nursery ownership semantics. When swapping objects between nursery and tenured heaps, the buffer ownership metadata can become inconsistent with the object's heap location, causing the GC to incorrectly free the buffer. The secondary issue is that shifted elements (array elements that have been logically removed from the front) are not accounted for when copying the buffer.

fix_commit_message:
Bug 1941876 - Fix handling of dynamic elements when swapping objects r=jandem

There are two problems here. Firstly, swapping a nursery and a tenured object
can leave dynamic element buffers with the wrong ownership kind. For example
we could have a tenured object with a nursery-owned buffer. This could cause
UAF if the buffer we collected in the next nursery collection.

Secondly, the code to copy dynamic elements doesn't account for shifted
elements.

I added the testcase but also updated the testObjectSwap JSAPI test to catch
this problem. The change to BufferAllocator::checkChunkGCStateNotInUse is to
speed up this test.

related_locations.description: Function declaration missing 'other' parameter needed to check if swapping between nursery and tenured objects

findings.suggestion: The condition should check if the objects being swapped are in different memory regions (nursery vs tenured), not just whether the current buffer is in the nursery. When swapping between nursery and tenured objects, the buffer must be copied and marked with the correct ownership kind to match the destination object. Additionally, the function needs to account for shifted elements when copying the buffer.
findings.title: Use-After-Free due to incorrect buffer ownership during object swap

location.snippet:
memmove(newElements, elements, size);
      elements_ = newElements->elements();

findings.message: When copying dynamic element buffers during object swap, the code uses memmove with 'elements' (which points to the shifted position) rather than the unshifted header. Additionally, when assigning the new elements pointer, it does not account for the number of shifted elements. This causes the copied buffer to have an incorrect header pointer, leading to memory corruption when the shifted elements are accessed.
findings.suggestion: When copying the element buffer, use getUnshiftedElementsHeader() as the source, and when setting elements_, account for the number of shifted elements to point to the correct location in the new buffer.
findings.title: Shifted elements not accounted for during element buffer copy

fix_commit.message: Bug 1941876 - Fix handling of dynamic elements when swapping objects r=jandem

must_cover.reason: Contains the vulnerable code path where dynamic element buffers are only copied when physically inside the nursery (ChunkPtrIsInsideNursery check on line 1038), but fails to check buffer allocator ownership metadata. This misses cases where a tenured object has a buffer marked as nursery-owned, causing the buffer to be incorrectly freed during GC.

Orchestrates the object swap operation by calling prepareForSwap for both objects (lines 1304, 1307, 1312, 1315) and then fixupAfterSwap. Understanding this flow is essential to see that when swapping a nursery object with a tenured object, the tenured object can end up with a buffer pointer that has nursery ownership semantics even though the buffer is not in nursery memory.

Restores object state after swap but only handles slots correctly (lines 1093-1094). Lines 1097-1100 handle dynamic elements but rely on prepareForSwap having correctly saved the buffer. If prepareForSwap didn't copy a nursery-allocated buffer, fixupAfterSwap won't correct the issue, allowing the dangling pointer to persist.

Shows how element buffers are handled during nursery collection. This function allocates new tenured buffers (lines 931-941) and copies elements. A reviewer must understand that the GC will free nursery-allocated buffers after this, which is why the buffer ownership metadata must be consistent with the actual allocation site.

ground_truth.root_cause: The introduction of the buffer allocator for JSObject elements changed how dynamic element buffers are managed during object swaps. The new code only copies buffers when they are physically inside the nursery memory region, but fails to consider cases where a buffer is allocated via AllocBuffer with nursery ownership semantics. When swapping objects between nursery and tenured heaps, the buffer ownership metadata can become inconsistent with the object's heap location, causing the GC to incorrectly free the buffer. The secondary issue is that shifted elements (array elements that have been logically removed from the front) are not accounted for when copying the buffer.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix c0937884a036 on top of intro a0f1dba96115 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (RaceCondition): The `EnqueueReceivedMessageDispatch` function unconditionally uses `NS_DispatchToMainThread` to dispatch messages. However, when ServiceWorkerContainer is exposed on worker threads (via WorkerNavigator), this causes messages to be dispatched to the main thread instead of the worker thread. This results in a race condition where the worker's JS runtime may be accessed from the main thread while it's being used on the worker thread, leading to memory safety violations and potential exploitation. Root cause: When exposing ServiceWorkerContainer to worker threads in Bug 1131324, the code change removed `MOZ_ASSERT(NS_IsMainThread())` from `DispatchMessage()` to allow it to work on worker threads, but failed to update the corresponding `EnqueueReceivedMessageDispatch()` function. This function still used `NS_DispatchToMainThread`, causing messages to always be dispatched to the main thread regardless of which thread the ServiceWorkerContainer belongs to.

findings.message: The `EnqueueReceivedMessageDispatch` function unconditionally uses `NS_DispatchToMainThread` to dispatch messages. However, when ServiceWorkerContainer is exposed on worker threads (via WorkerNavigator), this causes messages to be dispatched to the main thread instead of the worker thread. This results in a race condition where the worker's JS runtime may be accessed from the main thread while it's being used on the worker thread, leading to memory safety violations and potential exploitation.

related_locations.description: DispatchMessage function receives messages from wrong thread, removed MOZ_ASSERT(NS_IsMainThread()) in this commit which should have been a warning sign

findings.suggestion: When exposing ServiceWorkerContainer to worker threads, the dispatch mechanism must dispatch to the current thread (the thread that owns the ServiceWorkerContainer), not unconditionally to the main thread. Use `NS_DispatchToCurrentThread` instead of `NS_DispatchToMainThread`.
findings.title: Thread-unsafe dispatch in ServiceWorkerContainer

fix_commit.author: Olli Pettay
fix_commit.message: Bug 1942169 - Dispatch messages to the current thread r=asuth

must_cover.reason: Contains the vulnerable code that unconditionally dispatches to the main thread using NS_DispatchToMainThread, regardless of whether the ServiceWorkerContainer belongs to a window (main thread) or worker (worker thread). This causes messages to be dispatched to the wrong thread when the container is on a worker, leading to race conditions where the worker's JS runtime may be accessed from the main thread while in use on the worker thread.

This function was modified in Bug 1131324 to support worker threads (MOZ_ASSERT(NS_IsMainThread()) was removed), but the corresponding caller EnqueueReceivedMessageDispatch was not updated. A reviewer must see that DispatchMessage can execute on worker threads but is being dispatched to the main thread unconditionally, creating a thread-safety violation. The function accesses JS context and global objects that must be accessed on the correct thread.

This function receives messages from service workers and calls EnqueueReceivedMessageDispatch. A reviewer must understand that this function can be called on either the main thread (for window contexts) or worker threads (for worker contexts), and the dispatching must respect the current thread context. The function makes no thread checks before calling the vulnerable dispatch function.

This function exposes ServiceWorkerContainer on worker threads via WorkerNavigator.serviceWorker, making it accessible in worker contexts. This is the code path introduced in Bug 1131324 that enabled the vulnerability. A reviewer must understand that ServiceWorkerContainer can now exist on worker threads, not just main thread, which makes the thread-agnostic dispatch critical.

This function delivers messages to ServiceWorkerContainer by calling container->ReceiveMessage(). A reviewer must understand that this call can occur on any thread (main or worker) depending on where the ServiceWorkerContainer lives. The function operates on the thread owning the ClientSource/global object, which can be a worker thread, triggering the race condition when the message is incorrectly dispatched to the main thread.

ground_truth.root_cause: When exposing ServiceWorkerContainer to worker threads in Bug 1131324, the code change removed `MOZ_ASSERT(NS_IsMainThread())` from `DispatchMessage()` to allow it to work on worker threads, but failed to update the corresponding `EnqueueReceivedMessageDispatch()` function. This function still used `NS_DispatchToMainThread`, causing messages to always be dispatched to the main thread regardless of which thread the ServiceWorkerContainer belongs to.

pr_description: Differential Revision: https://phabricator.services.mozilla.com/D213725
pr_title: Bug 1131324 - Expose ServiceWorkerContainer on WorkerNavigator. r=dom-worker-reviewers,webidl,smaug

agent_reasoning: The bug-introducing commit added PipeWire video-capture support with the cleanup order reversed in ~PipeWireNode(): pw_proxy_destroy(proxy_) was called first, freeing the proxy and its listener_list, before spa_hook_remove(&node_listener_) ran. Since the hook internally references the proxy's listener_list, the subsequent spa_hook_remove() would access freed memory — a use-after-free. The fix swaps the two lines so the hook is removed while the proxy (and its listener_list) is still alive, then the proxy is safely destroyed.

pr_description:
When destroying a PipeWire camera node, the spa hook must be removed before the proxy object is destroyed. The hook is associated with the proxy's listener_list; destroying the proxy first frees that list while the hook still holds a reference to it. Calling spa_hook_remove() afterwards would then access freed memory.

This change corrects the destruction order in PipeWireNode::~PipeWireNode() so that spa_hook_remove() is called before pw_proxy_destroy(), ensuring the hook is cleanly unregistered from the still-valid proxy before the proxy is torn down.
pr_title: PipeWire camera: Fix cleanup order to avoid use-after-free

findings.message: The destructor calls pw_proxy_destroy() before spa_hook_remove(), which destroys the proxy object before removing the hook that is associated with it. The hook contains a listener_list reference (proxy->listener_list) that is freed when pw_proxy_destroy() is called. The subsequent spa_hook_remove() then attempts to access this freed memory to remove the hook from the list, causing a use-after-free vulnerability.
findings.suggestion: Swap the order of cleanup operations: remove the hook first before destroying the proxy object, since the hook is associated with the proxy and its listener_list.
findings.title: Use-After-Free due to incorrect cleanup order in PipeWireNode destructor

fix_commit.message: Bug 1942551 - WebRTC backport: PipeWire camera: Fix cleanup order r=pehrsons,webrtc-reviewers

must_cover.reason: Contains the vulnerable cleanup sequence where pw_proxy_destroy() is called before spa_hook_remove(). The proxy destruction frees the listener_list that the hook still references, causing use-after-free when spa_hook_remove() tries to access it.

Constructor establishes the data dependency between proxy_ and node_listener_. Line 99-100 creates the proxy via pw_registry_bind, and line 108-109 registers the hook listener on that proxy using pw_node_add_listener. This shows the hook is tied to the proxy's lifetime and requires the proxy to remain valid during hook removal.

Triggers destruction of PipeWireNode objects via std::erase_if on nodes_ vector. When a unique_ptr<PipeWireNode, PipeWireNodeDeleter> is erased, it invokes the custom deleter containing the vulnerable cleanup sequence. This is a key path that exercises the bug during device removal.

ground_truth.root_cause: Incorrect destruction order in resource cleanup. The hook is associated with the proxy object and internally references the proxy's listener_list. By destroying the proxy first, the listener_list is freed, but the hook still holds a dangling reference to it. When spa_hook_remove() tries to remove the hook from the list, it accesses freed memory.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 8354ae880cf5 on top of intro 9385dab26b90 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (TypeConfusion): The change to emitGuardIsNumber removed automatic conversion of Int32/Float32 inputs to Double. This broke an implicit assumption in visitSign that when input and output types differ, the input is always Double and output is Int32. When MSign now receives Int32 input with Double output, the else branch incorrectly asserts the opposite and uses LSignDI (Double input, Int32 output) instead of a proper LSignID (Int32 input, Double output). This causes: 1) Writing to an unrelated general purpose register instead of the allocated float output register, 2) The allocated float register retains its previous value, enabling type confusion where uninitialized/stale float data can be read as legitimate values. Root cause: The change in emitGuardIsNumber (bug 1941826) removed automatic conversion of Int32/Float32 inputs to Double for number guards. This was intended to enable better Float32 optimizations. However, downstream code in visitSign had hardcoded assumptions that when MSign input and output types differ, the input is always Double and output is Int32. The change created a new valid case (Int32 input, Double output) that was not handled, causing assertion failures and type confusion when the wrong LIR instruction was selected.

findings.message: The change to emitGuardIsNumber removed automatic conversion of Int32/Float32 inputs to Double. This broke an implicit assumption in visitSign that when input and output types differ, the input is always Double and output is Int32. When MSign now receives Int32 input with Double output, the else branch incorrectly asserts the opposite and uses LSignDI (Double input, Int32 output) instead of a proper LSignID (Int32 input, Double output). This causes: 1) Writing to an unrelated general purpose register instead of the allocated float output register, 2) The allocated float register retains its previous value, enabling type confusion where uninitialized/stale float data can be read as legitimate values.
findings.suggestion: When removing the automatic type conversion in emitGuardIsNumber, all downstream consumers that rely on specific type combinations need to be audited and updated. The visitSign function in Lowering.cpp needs to handle the new case where input is Int32 and output is Double by adding a new LIR instruction (LSignID) and corresponding code generation.
findings.title: Missing type conversion case in visitSign causes JIT type confusion

findings.message: The visitSign function only handles two cases: (1) same input/output types, and (2) Double input with Int32 output. After the change in emitGuardIsNumber, a third case became possible: Int32 input with Double output. The assertions at lines 2100-2101 assume the impossible third case cannot happen, but it now can. When this case is hit, the code incorrectly creates an LSignDI instruction (for Double->Int32) when it should create an LSignID instruction (for Int32->Double). This register type mismatch leads to writing to wrong registers and type confusion.
findings.suggestion: Add explicit handling for the Int32 input / Double output case by creating a new LSignID LIR instruction and corresponding CodeGenerator visitor. The fix should enumerate all four possible type combinations explicitly rather than relying on implicit assumptions.
findings.title: Incomplete type handling in LIRGenerator::visitSign

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 6624852dc946 on top of intro 70014fe558dd via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (UninitializedMemory): The `UnsafePreContentIterator::Init()` method returns an `nsresult` that can indicate failure (e.g., if the range is invalid or collapsed). When the return value is not checked, a failed initialization leaves the iterator's internal pointers (`mCurNode`, `mFirst`, `mLast`, `mClosestCommonInclusiveAncestor`) uninitialized. Subsequently calling `iter.IsDone()` and `iter.Next()` on this uninitialized iterator will dereference garbage or poison pointer values, leading to crashes or potential use-after-free conditions. Root cause: The root cause is twofold: (1) The `ContentIteratorBase` class did not default-initialize its internal pointer members (`mCurNode`, `mFirst`, `mLast`, `mClosestCommonInclusiveAncestor`), leaving them with indeterminate values when `Init()` fails. (2) The calling code in `SelectionNodeCache::MaybeCollect()` did not check the return value of `iter.Init(range)` before using the iterator, allowing the code to proceed with an improperly initialized iterator.
commit_message:
[Merged] Bug 1867249, part 1: Implemented new cache to determine selected nodes. r=sefeng,dom-core

Determining if a node is selected is a super-hot code path,
which at times introduces jank both in Reflow and Painting.
This is due to each node comparing its position to the range's start and end point,
which even happens several times (`nsINode::IsSelected()` and `Selection::LookupSelection()`).
In worst cases, this can lead to reflow which takes several minutes.

This patch introduces a cache which contains all fully selected nodes,
and lives throughout one `PresShell::DoReflow()` call.
Collecting all selected nodes of a selection is very fast.
The selected nodes are then stored in a hash set.
During reflow the check if a node is selected first checks the cache
if the node is fully selected, and otherwise goes through the existing
code to check if the node is partially selected.

Subsequently calling `iter.IsDone()` and `iter.Next()` on this uninitialized iterator will dereference garbage or poison pointer values, leading to crashes or potential use-after-free conditions.

related_locations.description: Uninitialized pointer members in ContentIteratorBase class

findings.suggestion: Check the return value of `iter.Init(range)` and skip iteration if it fails. The iterator's internal pointers should also be default-initialized to nullptr to make failed initializations safer.
findings.title: Unchecked return value of iterator initialization leads to use of uninitialized memory

findings.message: The `ContentIteratorBase` class declares raw pointer members (`mCurNode`, `mFirst`, `mLast`, `mClosestCommonInclusiveAncestor`) without default initialization. When the `Init()` method fails early (e.g., due to invalid range boundaries), these pointers retain their indeterminate values. Since `IsDone()` checks `!mCurNode` and `GetCurrentNode()` returns `mCurNode`, using an iterator after a failed `Init()` call leads to accessing garbage memory.
findings.suggestion: Default-initialize all pointer members to nullptr. Additionally, add [[nodiscard]] attribute to Init() methods to enforce checking return values at compile time.

agent_reasoning: The bug-introducing commit (Bug 1937634) made mStylesheetDocument a RefPtr AND added it to the NS_IMPL_CYCLE_COLLECTION_WRAPPERCACHE macro. The vulnerability arises because the macro's auto-generated UNLINK handler simply nulls out the RefPtr without first calling RemoveMutationObserver(this). This leaves the document holding a dangling pointer to a freed txMozillaXSLTProcessor as a mutation observer, causing a use-after-free when the document later notifies observers. The benign version keeps the RefPtr (the useful ownership semantic) but deliberately omits mStylesheetDocument from the cycle-collection macro. Bug 1937634 - Make txMozillaXSLTProcessor::mStylesheetDocument strong. r=peterv

Differential Revision: https://phabricator.services.mozilla.com/D232262
pr_description:
## Summary

`txMozillaXSLTProcessor::mStylesheetDocument` was previously a raw (weak) pointer to a `Document`. This PR converts it to a `RefPtr<mozilla::dom::Document>` to ensure the processor holds a proper owning reference for the lifetime of its association with the stylesheet document.

Previously the raw pointer carried an implicit assumption that some other owner would keep the document alive for the duration of the XSLT processor's use. Using a `RefPtr` makes that ownership explicit and avoids the risk of the document being freed while the processor still holds a reference to it.

The member is intentionally not added to the cycle-collection participant list: the XSLT processor registers itself as a mutation observer on the document via `AddMutationObserver(this)` in `ImportStylesheet()` and deregisters in the corresponding cleanup paths. Participating in cycle collection for this member would require a custom unlink handler to safely deregister the observer before the reference is cleared, which is not implemented here. The `RefPtr` alone is sufficient to guarantee lifetime safety without that complexity.

## Test plan

- [ ] Run existing XSLT-related tests (`dom/xslt/`)
- [ ] Verify no regressions in cycle-collector-related tests

findings.message: The change to make mStylesheetDocument a strong reference (RefPtr) added it to the NS_IMPL_CYCLE_COLLECTION_WRAPPERCACHE macro, which handles both traverse and unlink operations automatically. However, when the cycle collector unlinks mStylesheetDocument (sets it to null), it does not call RemoveMutationObserver(this) first. The txMozillaXSLTProcessor registers itself as a mutation observer on mStylesheetDocument via AddMutationObserver(this) in ImportStylesheet(). When the document is unlinked during cycle collection, the document still holds a dangling pointer to the txMozillaXSLTProcessor as a mutation observer. When the document is later destroyed and tries to notify observers, it accesses freed memory, causing a use-after-free crash in nsINode::LastRelease().
findings.suggestion: When using NS_IMPL_CYCLE_COLLECTION_WRAPPERCACHE with mStylesheetDocument, a separate UNLINK handler must be implemented that calls mStylesheetDocument->RemoveMutationObserver(this) before the reference is cleared. The correct approach is to use NS_IMPL_CYCLE_COLLECTION_WRAPPERCACHE_CLASS with separate UNLINK_BEGIN/END and TRAVERSE_BEGIN/END macros, where UNLINK calls Reset() or explicitly removes the mutation observer before unlinking the document reference.

NS_IMPL_CYCLE_COLLECTION_WRAPPERCACHE_CLASS(txMozillaXSLTProcessor)

NS_IMPL_CYCLE_COLLECTION_UNLINK_BEGIN(txMozillaXSLTProcessor)
  NS_IMPL_CYCLE_COLLECTION_UNLINK(mOwner, mSource)
  MOZ_RELEASE_ASSERT(tmp->mState == State::None);
  tmp->Reset(IgnoreErrors());  // This calls RemoveMutationObserver
  NS_IMPL_CYCLE_COLLECTION_UNLINK_PRESERVED_WRAPPER
NS_IMPL_CYCLE_COLLECTION_UNLINK_END

NS_IMPL_CYCLE_COLLECTION_TRAVERSE_BEGIN(txMozillaXSLTProcessor)
  NS_IMPL_CYCLE_COLLECTION_TRAVERSE(
      mOwner, mStylesheetDocument, mEmbeddedStylesheetRoot, mSource, mVariables)
NS_IMPL_CYCLE_COLLECTION_TRAVERSE_END

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 6dbdf1fff1e0 on top of intro 492e6f8efcbc via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (DataRace): The EnsureLocale() function modifies mLocale member variable from the main thread without proper synchronization, while GetLocale() reads mLocale concurrently from worker threads. This creates a data race condition: the main thread can call EnsureLocale() multiple times (through IDBFactory::AllowedForWindowInternal, WorkerPrivate::GetLoadInfo, or RemoteWorkerChild::ExecWorkerOnMainThread), potentially reallocating the string buffer while DOM worker threads are reading it via GetLocale() called in IDBFactory::OpenInternal. This can lead to use-after-free or buffer overflow when the worker thread reads memory that has been freed or reallocated by the main thread. Root cause: The EnsureLocale() function was introduced without synchronization or idempotency protection. It can be called multiple times from different code paths (IDBFactory::AllowedForWindowInternal, WorkerPrivate::GetLoadInfo, RemoteWorkerChild::ExecWorkerOnMainThread), and each call modifies the shared mLocale member. Meanwhile, DOM worker threads read this member via GetLocale() without any synchronization, creating a classic writer-reader race condition.

findings.suggestion: Add a guard to prevent re-initialization of mLocale after it's been set. Introduce a boolean flag mLocaleInitialized and check it at the beginning of EnsureLocale() to return early if already initialized. Mark the flag with MOZ_GUARDED_BY for thread safety annotation.
findings.title: Data race on mLocale string member without synchronization

findings.message: EnsureLocale() is called from multiple locations without coordination: IDBFactory::AllowedForWindowInternal (main thread), WorkerPrivate::GetLoadInfo (main thread), and RemoteWorkerChild::ExecWorkerOnMainThread (main thread). While all these callers run on the main thread, DOM worker threads concurrently access GetLocale() which reads mLocale. The lack of synchronization between the writing main thread and reading worker threads creates a TOCTOU-style race where mLocale can be modified between the worker thread's check and use.
findings.suggestion: Ensure EnsureLocale() is idempotent by only initializing mLocale once. Once initialized, subsequent calls should be no-ops. This prevents the string buffer from being reallocated while worker threads may be reading it.

Vulnerability (UseAfterFree): The GetAction method returns a raw pointer to an nsIAlertAction object without properly incrementing its reference count. In XPIDL, output parameters with double-pointer types like `nsIAlertAction** aAlertAction` expect the callee to transfer ownership by incrementing the reference count. The current implementation directly assigns the raw pointer (`*aAlertAction = action`) without calling AddRef(). When the caller uses getter_AddRefs(), it expects to receive an already-incremented reference which it will later release. This mismatch causes the reference count to become incorrect: the object's ref count stays the same, but the caller will decrement it when done, potentially freeing the object while other references still exist, leading to a use-after-free vulnerability. Root cause: The developer directly assigned the raw pointer from the RefPtr in the mActions array to the output parameter without understanding that XPIDL getter semantics require transferring ownership via AddRef/forget. The pattern `*aAlertAction = action` does not increment the reference count, while the expected pattern is to create a RefPtr copy and call forget() on it.

fix_commit.message: Bug 1951154 - Fix AlertNotification::GetAction r=asuth

must_cover.reason: Contains the vulnerable code where a raw pointer from mActions array is directly assigned to the output parameter (*aAlertAction = action) without incrementing the reference count. XPIDL getters with double-pointer output parameters require AddRef() or forget() to transfer ownership, but this implementation omits it, causing incorrect reference counting that leads to use-after-free.

Calls GetAction at line 582 within a loop iterating over mActions. This caller expects to receive a properly reference-counted object (via getter_AddRefs semantics) which it will later release. The incorrect reference count from GetAction causes the object to be prematurely freed when this caller releases it, while other references may still exist.

Calls GetAction at line 903 to retrieve an action object based on user interaction. This caller also expects proper reference counting via getter_AddRefs semantics. When it releases the object after use, the reference count will drop below what it should be, potentially freeing the object while it's still referenced elsewhere in the mActions array.

Demonstrates the correct pattern for XPIDL getters returning COM objects via double-pointer parameters. Comparing GetPrincipal (which likely uses NS_IF_ADDREF or forget()) with GetAction reveals the missing reference count increment in GetAction. This comparison is essential for understanding what GetAction should do.

ground_truth.root_cause: The developer directly assigned the raw pointer from the RefPtr in the mActions array to the output parameter without understanding that XPIDL getter semantics require transferring ownership via AddRef/forget. The pattern `*aAlertAction = action` does not increment the reference count, while the expected pattern is to create a RefPtr copy and call forget() on it.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix d3c35516e9e8 on top of intro 52d7d34ee0f9 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (DataRace): The `GetConnInfo()` method reads `mConnInfo` on the main thread without holding a lock, while `DisableHttp3()` modifies `mConnInfo` via `mConnInfo.swap(connInfo)` on the socket thread. This creates a data race condition. The ThreadSanitizer detected a read of size 8 on the main thread in `GetConnInfo` concurrent with a write of size 8 on thread T7 in `DisableHttp3`. This can lead to use-after-free or reading corrupted pointer values, potentially causing crashes or undefined behavior. Root cause: Bug 1948203 introduced a new call to mTransaction->GetConnInfo() in nsHttpChannel::ContinueProcessResponse1() on the main thread to pass connection information to ProcessAltService(). However, mConnInfo in nsHttpTransaction was already being modified by DisableHttp3() on the socket thread without synchronization. The pre-existing code paths didn't have this cross-thread access pattern, making the race condition a regression introduced by this optimization patch.
commit_message:
[Merged] Bug 1948203 - Skip alt-svc validation if we already connected to the server, r=necko-reviewers,jesup

This patch optimizes how Firefox handles speculative connections for alt-svc headers. When a server sends an alt-svc header, Firefox normally creates a speculative connection to validate it. With this patch, if the connection’s hash key matches the one generated from the alt-svc header, the validation step is skipped since an equivalent connection is already in place, avoiding unnecessary work.

findings.suggestion: Access to mConnInfo must be synchronized. The fix introduces a `mFinalizedConnInfo` member that is a clone of `mConnInfo` taken when the transaction is activated. findings.message: The `GetConnInfo()` method in `nsHttpTransaction` accesses the `mConnInfo` member variable without any synchronization primitive (mutex lock). This is called from the main thread in `ContinueProcessResponse1()`, but `mConnInfo` can be modified by `DisableHttp3()` running on the socket thread via `mConnInfo.swap(connInfo)`. The RefPtr::Clone() operation dereferences the pointer, which races with the swap operation that modifies the pointer itself.
findings.suggestion: Add mutex protection when accessing mConnInfo, or use a separate finalized copy that's taken at a safe point during transaction activation and accessed under lock protection.
findings.title: Unprotected access to shared mConnInfo member

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix c8463bc87470 on top of intro 3cd1bb82abdd via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (WildPointer): When calculating the calleePtr in createManyLazyEntryStubs, the code uses `tierCodeBlock.segment->base()` instead of `tierCodeBlock.base()`. This commit changed the semantics of all code offsets to be relative to CodeBlock::codeBase instead of segment->base(), but this particular location was missed. When the CodeBlock's codeBase differs from the segment base (which can happen when multiple code blocks share a segment), the calculated calleePtr will point to the wrong memory location. This causes the generated wasm entry stub to call an incorrect code pointer, potentially resulting in execution of arbitrary or unintended code within the module's code range. Root cause: During the refactoring in bug 1861078 to make metadata offsets relative to CodeBlock::codeBase instead of segment->base(), one location in createManyLazyEntryStubs was not updated. The segmentBase variable continued to use tierCodeBlock.segment->base() when it should have used tierCodeBlock.base(). Since CodeBlock::codeBase can differ from segment->base() (multiple code blocks can share a segment with different offsets), using the wrong base results in calculating an incorrect calleePtr that points to the wrong code location.

findings.message: The `readAllocSiteIndex()` function appends to a vector using `masm.append(wasm::AllocSitePatch())` but does not check if the append operation succeeded. findings.suggestion: The function should return a boolean to indicate success/failure and use an out parameter for the index. The OOM condition from masm.append() must be checked before returning the index. All callers must check the return value and handle the OOM case by returning false to propagate the error up the call stack.

agent_reasoning: The vulnerability was a use-after-free in the GC string promotion path. When a dependent string's root base was already tenured or promoted to tospace (i.e., NOT in the collected nursery region), the old code skipped calling `setBase()` on the promoted dependent string. This left the `d.s.u3.base` field pointing to the original (pre-promotion) base pointer from `rootBaseDuringMinorGC()`, which could be a stale intermediate chain node rather than the actual promoted root base. Subsequent GC tracing of the base chain would then follow a dangling pointer, causing a use-after-free. The fix ensures `setBase()` is always called with the actual promoted root base, completely eliminating the asymmetric handling that caused the stale pointer. The additional `maybeCloneCharsOnPromotionTyped` fixes (condition change and nursery malloc registration) prevent related memory safety issues when cloning dependent string chars during promotions in semispace nursery collections.

[Merged] Bug 1959310 - Single-pass string deduplication r=jonco  - Remove order-dependence between dependent strings and their bases by force-promoting their root base strings rather than using separate fixup phases (and different fixups for nursery and...

 - Force-promotion is a recursive call, but it is guaranteed to bottom out immediately because root bases are never themselves dependent strings.
 - Remove the aforementioned fixup phases (the nursery one still exists, but for recursing through ropes only)
 - Clone the original characters (which will not yet have been freed or poisoned) in the event that a promoted nursery string can't recover its original characters pointer

pr_description:
When promoting a dependent string during minor GC, the root base pointer stored in the dependent string's `d.s.u3.base` field must always be updated to point to the actual promoted root base — regardless of whether the root base was in the collected nursery region or had already been tenured/promoted.

Previously, when the root base was NOT in the collected nursery region, `promoteString` only forwarded the source string without calling `setBase()` to update the dependent string's base pointer. Because `rootBaseDuringMinorGC()` may traverse an intermediate chain that differs from the dependent string's direct base pointer, the base field could retain a stale pointer after promotion.

This change restructures the dependent string promotion path in `promoteString` to always call `setBase()` with the actual promoted root base, then conditionally call `updateToPromotedBase()` only when the base was in the collected region. The store buffer post-barrier is handled implicitly by `setBase()`.

Additionally, `maybeCloneCharsOnPromotionTyped` is updated to:
- Use `InCollectedNurseryRegion(root)` instead of `!root->isTenured()` for the early-return check, which correctly handles semispace nursery collections where a string may be in tospace but not yet tenured.
- Properly register malloc'd clone buffers with the nursery when the promoted string is not yet tenured, instead of only calling `addCellMemory` (which is only valid for tenured cells).

The `maybeCloneCharsOnPromotion` helper is simplified to `void` return type since the cloned byte count was being double-counted against tenured promotion totals (the donor string still owns those bytes and may still be alive).

findings.message: The allocateBuffer function calculates numBytes using calcAllocSize which can produce very large size_t values. While calcAllocSize uses CheckedInt to detect overflow within size_t, there is no check that the resulting size fits within uint32_t before passing to allocateCellBuffer. This allows the code path to proceed with a truncated size value when the actual required buffer exceeds 4GB.
findings.suggestion: Add an explicit check that numBytes fits within the range expected by allocateCellBuffer, or add capacity limits to prevent the hash table from growing to sizes that would cause overflow.

pr_description:
In `TRRServiceChannel::OnStartRequest()`, obtain the connection info atomically via `TakeResponseHeadAndConnInfo()` rather than calling `TakeResponseHead()` for the response head and then `GetConnInfo()` separately for the connection info.

Vulnerability (UseAfterFree): When rendering without presenting (present=false), the code skips calling mCompositor->BeginFrame(), which is responsible for calling MakeCurrent() to initialize the GL context. This causes wr_renderer_update() and wr_renderer_render() to execute OpenGL operations without a valid GL context being current. On systems with NVIDIA drivers, this can lead to the driver accessing freed memory or incorrect GL state, resulting in a use-after-free crash. The crash signature shows the issue occurs in libgdk-3.so.0 gdk_x11_app_launch_context_get_type, triggered during WebRender operations involving NVIDIA EGL libraries. Root cause: The bug was introduced in Bug 1961115 which added a 'present' flag to skip compositor work when rendering offscreen content. The original code always called mCompositor->BeginFrame() which internally calls MakeCurrent() to establish the GL context. After the change, when present=false, neither BeginFrame() nor MakeCurrent() was called, leaving the GL context in an undefined state. Subsequent calls to wr_renderer_update() and wr_renderer_render() then operate without a valid GL context, causing NVIDIA EGL drivers to potentially access freed or invalid memory.

fix_commit.message: Bug 1973975 - Ensure that glMakeCurrent is called when rendering without presenting. r=gfx-reviewers,aosmond

must_cover.reason: Contains the vulnerable control flow where present=false skips both BeginFrame() (line 198-227) and the fallback MakeCurrent() call (line 228-230 only executes when beginFrame=true but present=false). When present=false and beginFrame=true, execution reaches line 242 wr_renderer_update() without any GL context initialization, causing UAF when NVIDIA drivers access uninitialized GL state.

BeginFrame() is the normal path that calls MakeCurrent() (line 61) to initialize the GL context. Understanding that BeginFrame() performs this critical initialization is necessary to recognize that skipping it when present=false leaves the GL context uninitialized, enabling the UAF vulnerability.

Shows the correct pattern: Update() properly guards wr_renderer_update() call with MakeCurrent() check (line 164). This establishes that wr_renderer_update() requires a valid GL context. Comparing this with UpdateAndRender() reveals that UpdateAndRender() violates this invariant when present=false, making the bug detectable.

ground_truth.root_cause: The bug was introduced in Bug 1961115 which added a 'present' flag to skip compositor work when rendering offscreen content. The original code always called mCompositor->BeginFrame() which internally calls MakeCurrent() to establish the GL context. After the change, when present=false, neither BeginFrame() nor MakeCurrent() was called, leaving the GL context in an undefined state. agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 2b8155c2c4c2 on top of intro 321172222a2e via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (OutOfBoundsRead): FinalizationRegistryObject::unregister() in SpiderMonkey reads its first argument using the unchecked CallArgs::operator[] (`args[0]`) before validating that an argument was actually supplied, instead of using the bounds-safe `args.get(0)`. Calling `FinalizationRegistry.prototype.unregister` with zero arguments (e.g. `new FinalizationRegistry(()=>{}).unregister()`) causes an out-of-bounds read of the native call's argument vector, tripping a debug assertion (`i < argc_` in js/public/CallArgs.h) and causing undefined behavior / a security-relevant OOB read in release/optimized builds. Root cause: Bug 1863140 Part 3 (commit 321172222a2e) refactored FinalizationRegistry.register/unregister to support non-object (e.g. symbol) targets/unregister tokens via a new CanBeHeldWeakly() helper. While doing so, the unregister() function's existing safe pattern of `args.get(0).isObject()` followed by `&args[0].toObject()` (indexing only after confirming the argument existed and was an object) was replaced by directly constructing `RootedValue unregisterToken(cx, args[0])` ahead of any validation, re-introducing an unchecked array index into the native call arguments before verifying argc covers that index.

findings.message: As part of adding symbol-target support for FinalizationRegistry (Bug 1863140 Part 3), the code in FinalizationRegistryObject::unregister was refactored to accept non-object unregister tokens (via CanBeHeldWeakly) by first fetching the raw argument with `args[0]` into a RootedValue, and only afterwards validating it with CanBeHeldWeakly(). Previously the code validated `args.get(0).isObject()` (a bounds-safe accessor that returns UndefinedValue when the argument is missing) before ever indexing into args. By moving the unchecked `args[0]` access ahead of the validation, calling `FinalizationRegistry.prototype.unregister()` with zero arguments causes CallArgs::operator[] to be invoked with index 0 while argc_ is 0, tripping the `MOZ_ASSERT(i < argc_)` bounds assertion in js/public/CallArgs.h (and in non-debug/release builds, an out-of-bounds read of the arguments vector). The fix (Bug 1987290) replaces `args[0]` with the bounds-safe `args.get(0)`, which returns JS::UndefinedValue when argc is insufficient instead of indexing out of bounds.
findings.suggestion: Use the bounds-safe CallArgs::get() accessor instead of operator[] when the argument is optional / argc is not yet validated. get(0) returns UndefinedValue() when argc is 0 (or less than the requested index), avoiding any out-of-bounds access, and CanBeHeldWeakly(UndefinedValue) correctly evaluates to false so the existing TypeError path is still taken when no token is supplied.

agent_reasoning:
Without this change, GetBufferSource captures a raw SharedMem<uint8_t*> pointer+length into the caller-supplied ArrayBuffer/typed-array's backing store, and only afterward do WebAssembly.compile/instantiate/validate/Module() call FeatureOptions::init on the second (options) argument. Since that argument can be a Proxy, FeatureOptions::init can trigger arbitrary user JS (via trap handlers), which can detach the original buffer (e.g. ArrayBuffer.prototype.transfer()) or otherwise free its backing store. The wasm decoder then reads through the now-dangling pointer, a use-after-free read reachable from pure JS.

The fix reorders each entry point so FeatureOptions::init runs before the bytecode source is captured, and wraps every subsequent raw-pointer read (synchronous CompileBuffer/Validate calls, and BytecodeBuffer::fromSource's copy for the async paths) in an AutoPinBufferSourceLength guard that pins the buffer's length for the duration, causing any detach/resize attempt during that window to fail cleanly (JS::PinArrayBufferOrViewLength) instead of leaving a dangling pointer to be read. This restores the safety property that existed before bug 1931407's refactor to non-owning BytecodeSource, without reintroducing the eager bytecode copies that refactor was meant to avoid.
commit_message:
Bug 1931407 - wasm: Rework bytecode handling for compilation to avoid copies. r=yury

We have two problems in bytecode handling:
  1. When streaming compiling, we have dis-contiguous buffers for 'env' 'code' and 'tail'
     regions of bytecode that we parse. This is because while we're background compiling
     the code section we cannot resize that buffer, and so we have a separate 'tail'
     buffer for those bytes as they come off of the wire. However ModuleGenerator::
     finishModule requires the bytecode to be contiguous so we make a big copy of the
     whole module.
      - Then this copy is thrown away if we're not tiering.
      - For eager tiering, we actually create a new copy of just the code section and
        break the bytecode back apart to what we originally had.
  2. When we're doing a synchronous compile, we make a copy of the module bytecode from
     the original array buffer. However there's no need to do this and we could actually
     just decode directly from the array buffer memory.

This commit fixes (1) by switching all of our bytecode handling to work on the (env, code,
tail) version of bytecode and not assume it is contiguous. This is abstracted away in a
new BytecodeSource class which handles the details.

We can fix (2) by making BytecodeSource just have a weak reference to the bytecode, and
adding a BytecodeBuffer class which actually owns the buffers. When we sync compile, we
just use BytecodeSource and never construct a BytecodeBuffer.

findings.message: WebAssembly_validate (and the sibling WasmModuleObject::construct / WebAssembly_compile paths) call GetBufferSource() first, which unwraps the user-supplied BufferSource object and stores a *raw, non-owning* pointer/length pair (BytecodeSource) directly into the ArrayBuffer's backing data via SharedMem<uint8_t*> dataPointer. Previously (before this commit) GetBufferSource eagerly copied the bytes into an owned ShareableBytes, so any later detach was harmless. After this refactor ('Rework bytecode handling ... to avoid copies'), BytecodeSource is just a weak reference with no copy at this point. Immediately afterward, the code calls FeatureOptions::init(cx, callArgs.get(1)), which can invoke arbitrary JS (e.g. a Proxy 'get' trap on the second argument object while reading the 'builtins' property). That user-controlled callback can call ArrayBuffer.prototype.transfer() on the same buffer referenced by `source`, detaching it and freeing/invalidating the data pointer. The subsequent call to Validate(cx, source, options, &error) (and, in other call sites, CompileBuffer) then dereferences the dangling pointer, leading to a use-after-free read that crashes in js::wasm::DecodeModuleEnvironment when parsing the freed bytes.
findings.suggestion: Either (a) obtain/parse FeatureOptions before grabbing the raw bytecode pointer so any detach happens prior to taking the reference, and/or (b) pin the ArrayBuffer/view's length (JS::PinArrayBufferOrViewLength) for the duration of compilation/validation so it cannot be detached while BytecodeSource/BytecodeBuffer holds a weak reference to it, releasing the pin once compilation completes.
findings.title: Use-after-free: wasm bytecode pointer captured before FeatureOptions::init can detach the backing buffer

The new code paths then call into user-controllable JS (FeatureOptions::init, which parses an options object that can be a Proxy) after capturing the raw pointer but before using it, creating a window where the buffer can be detached/freed out from under the still-held pointer.

findings.message: In StableWasmArrayObjectElements::StableWasmArrayObjectElements(), when a WasmArrayObject stores its data inline, the code copies the inline array data into a heap Vector sized to hold exactly numElements_ elements of type T. The call `std::copy(array->inlineStorage(), array->inlineStorage() + array->numElements_ * sizeof(T), ownElements_->begin())` passes a byte-typed (uint8_t*) source range whose length is expressed in bytes (numElements_ * sizeof(T)) but a T-typed destination iterator. std::copy advances the source and destination iterators in lockstep and performs exactly (last - first) iterations — here that is numElements_ * sizeof(T) iterations, each writing one element to the destination. Because the destination iterator is T* (not uint8_t*), each iteration advances the destination pointer by sizeof(T) bytes, so the loop writes sizeof(T) times more T-sized slots than the vector actually holds (which was resized to only numElements_ elements). This causes an out-of-bounds write past the end of the destination Vector's storage whenever sizeof(T) > 1, i.e. for every element type wider than a single byte. Additionally, the source pointer `array->inlineStorage()` points to the start of the inline storage region (which includes the DataHeader), not to `offsetOfInlineArrayData()` where the actual array element data begins, so even the bytes read are from the wrong offset. The overall effect is a heap-based buffer overflow write (and incorrect data source) reachable from WebAssembly GC array operations that use StableWasmArrayObjectElements, matching the reported 'incorrect boundary conditions' WebAssembly memory-safety vulnerability.
findings.suggestion: Use a source iterator with element type T that points at the correct array-data offset (offsetOfInlineArrayData(), not offsetOfInlineStorage()) and express the copy length in elements, not bytes, so that std::copy's source and destination iterators have matching, consistently-typed strides. Add a helper such as `T* inlineArrayElements()` that returns `offsetToPointer<T>(offsetOfInlineArrayData())`, then call `std::copy(src, src + array->numElements_, ownElements_->begin())`.
findings.suggestion_code:
const T* src = array->inlineArrayElements<T>();
std::copy(src, src + array->numElements_, ownElements_->begin());
findings.title: Heap buffer overflow from mismatched std::copy iterator types in StableWasmArrayObjectElements

must_cover.reason: Primary location of finding: Heap buffer overflow from mismatched std::copy iterator types in StableWasmArrayObjectElements

ground_truth.root_cause: Type confusion between a byte-granularity source iterator (uint8_t*) with a byte-count length and an element-granularity destination iterator (T*) passed to std::copy, causing the loop trip count (computed as last-first in the source's element type) to be interpreted as T-sized elements against the destination, over-writing the destination buffer by sizeof(T)x.

agent_reasoning:
The bug-introducing commit (bug 1777800) rewrote escapeStringWin to use an allow-list based negated regex (`[^a-zA-Z0-9\s_\-:=+~\/.',?;()*\$&\\{}\"`]`) to decide which characters get the `^` escape prefix for cmd.exe. This regex used the `\s` shorthand, which is broader than a literal space and lets tab/form-feed/vertical-tab/unicode whitespace pass through unescaped, enabling command/argument injection when such characters appear in attacker-controlled network data reflected into the generated curl command.

The fix commit (bug 1996761) addresses the equivalent issue in a later, differently-structured version of the same file by inserting a new `.replace(/[^\S\r\n]/g, " ")` step that normalizes all whitespace other than line breaks to a literal space before further processing. I applied the same conceptual fix directly to the on-disk `escapeStringWin` function (as it exists at the intro commit), inserting the whitespace-normalization replace at the equivalent point in the escaping pipeline: after the `%`-escaping step and before the newline normalization/escaping steps, since line breaks are handled separately. This closes off the same whitespace-passthrough vulnerability without altering the surrounding escaping logic or line-break handling.

-       variable value. So %% becomes "%""%". Even if an env variable ""
-       (2 doublequotes) is declared, the cmd.exe will not
-       substitute it with its value.

-       Replace each backslash with double backslash to make sure
-       MS Crt arguments parser won't collapse them.
-
-       Replace new line outside of quotes since cmd.exe doesn't let
-       to do it inside. At the same time it gets duplicated,
-       because first newline is consumed by ^.
-       So for quote: `"Text-start\r\ntext-continue"`,
-       we get: `"Text-start"^\r\n\r\n"text-continue"`,
-       where `^\r\n` is just breaking the command, the `\r\n` right
-       after is actual escaped newline.
+      Because cmd.exe parser and MS Crt arguments parsers use some of the
+      same escape characters, they can interact with each other in
+      horrible ways, the order of operations is critical.
     */
+    const encapsChars = '"';
     return (
-      '"' +
+      encapsChars +
       str
-        .replaceAll("`", "``")
-        .replaceAll("$", "`$")
-        .replaceAll('"', '""')
-        .replaceAll("%", '"%"')
+
+        //  Replace \ with \\ first because it is an escape character for certain
+        // conditions in both parsers.
         .replace(/\\/g, "\\\\")
-        .replace(/[\r\n]{1,2}/g, '"^$&$&"') +
-      '"'
+
+        // Replace double quote chars with two double quotes (not by escaping with \") because it is
+        // recognized by both cmd.exe and MS Crt arguments parser.
+        .replace(/"/g, '""')
+
+        // Escape ` and $ so commands do not get executed e.g $(calc.exe) or `\$(calc.exe)
+        .replace(/[`$]/g, "\\$&")
+
+        // Then escape all characters we are not sure about with ^ to ensure it
+        // gets to MS Crt parser safely.
+        .replace(/[^a-zA-Z0-9\s_\-:=+~\/.',?;()*\$&\\{}\"`]/g, "^$&")
+
+        // The % character is special because MS Crt parser will try and look for
+        // ENV variables and fill them in its place. We cannot escape them with %
+        // and cannot escape them with ^ (because it's cmd.exe's escape not MS Crt
+        // parser); So we can get cmd.exe parser to escape the character after it,
+        // if it is followed by a valid beginning character of an ENV variable.
+        // This ensures we do not try and double escape another ^ if it was placed
+        // by the previous replace.
+        .replace(/%(?=[a-zA-Z0-9_])/g, "%^")

+        // All other whitespace characters are replaced with a single space, as there
+        // is no way to enter their literal values in a command line, and they do break

+        // Since want to keep line breaks, we need to exclude them in the regex (`[^\r\n]`),
+        // and use double negations to get the other whitespace chars (`[^\S]` translates
+        // to "not not whitespace")
+        .replace(/[^\S\r\n]/g, " ")
+
+        // We replace \r and \r\n with \n, this allows to consistently escape all new
+        // lines in the next replace
+        .replace(/\r\n?/g, "\n")
+
+        // Lastly we replace new lines with ^ and TWO new lines because the first
+        // new line is there to enact the escape command the second is the character
+        // to escape (in this case new line).
+        // The extra " enables escaping new lines with ^ within quotes in cmd.exe.
+        .replace(/\n/g, '"^\r\n\r\n"') +
+      encapsChars
     );
   },

-        .replace(/[\r\n]{1,2}/g, '"^$&$&"') +
-      '"'
+
+        // Replace double quote chars with two double quotes (not by escaping with \") because it is
+        // recognized by both cmd.exe and MS Crt arguments parser.
+        .replace(/"/g, '""')
+
+        // Escape ` and $ so commands do not get executed e.g $(calc.exe) or `\$(calc.exe)
+        .replace(/[`$]/g, "\\$&")
+

+        // gets to MS Crt parser safely.
+        .replace(/[^a-zA-Z0-9\s_\-:=+~\/.',?;()*\$&\\{}\"`]/g, "^$&")

+        // and cannot escape them with ^ (because it's cmd.exe's escape not MS Crt
+        // parser); So we can get cmd.exe parser to escape the character after it,
+        // if it is followed by a valid beginning character of an ENV variable.

+        // new line is there to enact the escape command the second is the character

findings.message: The Windows cmd.exe escaping routine used by the Network Monitor's "Copy as cURL" feature (CurlUtils.escapeStringWin) builds a character class of characters that are considered 'safe' and therefore NOT escaped with the cmd.exe caret (^) escape character. This character class includes the JavaScript regex shorthand `\s`, which matches not only the space character but also other whitespace-like control characters such as horizontal tab (\t, U+0009), form feed (\f, U+000C), vertical tab (\v, U+000B) and non-breaking/Unicode space variants. Because these characters are excluded from the escaping performed by `.replace(/[^a-zA-Z0-9\s_\-:=+~\/.',?;()*\$&\\{}\"`]/g, "^$&")`, any such control character present in attacker-controlled request data (e.g. a header name/value, URL, or body captured by the network panel) is copied through to the generated curl.exe command line unescaped. On Windows, cmd.exe/CRT argument parsing treats several of these whitespace-like characters as argument/token separators, so an attacker who can influence the value being copied (for example via a malicious response header or URL processed by the page under inspection) can break out of the intended single argument and inject additional command-line tokens/options into the curl.exe invocation that the user pastes into a shell, resulting in privilege escalation / command injection when the generated command is executed.
findings.suggestion: Do not include the `\s` shorthand (or otherwise leave whitespace/control characters unescaped) in the 'safe characters' negated character class used for cmd.exe escaping. Explicitly handle newlines separately (as the code already does) and escape or normalize all other whitespace-like characters (tab, form feed, vertical tab, unicode spaces, and other control/format characters) to a single literal space (or otherwise neutralize them) before they can reach the generated command line, since there is no way to represent their literal values safely on a Windows command line and they can be used to break argument boundaries.
findings.suggestion_code: .replace(/[^\S\r\n]/g, " ")
findings.title: Netmonitor "Copy as cURL (Windows)" fails to escape whitespace-like control characters, enabling command injection

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 2fa42593dec7 on top of intro 90711c04449c via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (LogicError): SpiderMonkey's IonMonkey JIT backend added an MIR peephole optimization, MGuardShape::foldsTo(), that removes a redundant MGuardShape instruction when its object operand is itself another MGuardShape checking the same shape. The optimization conflated syntactic operand/shape equality with semantic equivalence: it did not verify that the two guards share the same instruction dependency (i.e. that no shape-mutating effect could occur between them). A regressing change (Bug 1991402 Part 7, needed to avoid duplicate shape guards emitted for the new SetSize inline-cache IR) introduced this flawed foldsTo implementation. When user JS causes an object's shape to be mutated (e.g. by adding new properties or via a for-in loop inside a setter) between two otherwise-identical GuardShape instructions, the JIT incorrectly elides the second guard, allowing subsequent code to operate under a stale/incorrect shape assumption. This manifests as the debug assertion `slots == calculateDynamicSlots()` in NativeObject::numDynamicSlots, and represents a real object-layout type confusion in release builds exploitable for memory corruption. Root cause: MGuardShape::foldsTo() assumed that two MGuardShape instructions testing the same shape with the same object operand are always redundant to fold, without checking whether an intervening effectful instruction (recorded via the instruction's alias-set `dependency()`) could have mutated the object's shape between the two guards. Congruent shape and operand does not imply the absence of an intervening shape-mutating side effect in IonMonkey's non-SSA-effect representation; the dependency link exists precisely to encode that ordering, and foldsTo ignored it.

findings.message: MGuardShape::foldsTo() was added to fold away a redundant MGuardShape when its input operand is itself another MGuardShape testing the same shape. The optimization assumes that if two consecutive GuardShape instructions check the same shape, the second is always redundant and the object operand can be substituted directly. However, this reasoning only holds if the two guards are known to observe the object at the same point in the program's effectful ordering (same alias-set dependency). The implementation never checks `dependency()` / `object()->dependency()`, so if code motion, alias analysis, or an intervening side effect (e.g. shape-mutating property addition such as `this.m = 0; this.n = 0;` in a setter, or a `for...in` enumeration) was legally allowed to occur between the two GuardShape instructions, folding away the second guard can leave the JIT believing an object still has the shape proven by the first guard when the object's actual shape (and therefore dynamic slot layout) has since changed. Downstream code (e.g. NativeObject::growSlotsPure / numDynamicSlots) then operates on stale shape-derived slot-count assumptions, producing the `slots == calculateDynamicSlots()` assertion failure, and in a non-debug build a genuine object-layout/type confusion that can be exploited for memory corruption.
findings.suggestion: Only fold away the inner MGuardShape when the two guards are proven to observe the object at the same effectful point, i.e. require that both instructions have a recorded alias-set dependency and that they are equal (`dependency() && object()->dependency() == dependency()`), matching the later fix. Without this check, any intervening shape-mutating operation between the two guards invalidates the assumption that the first guard's proven shape still holds at the second guard's location.
findings.title: MGuardShape::foldsTo elides a shape guard without checking instruction dependency, allowing stale shape assumptions after shape mutation

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 0264cf850afd on top of intro 9bd0056bb97a via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (UseAfterFree): Bug 2003588 (CVE-2026-0884) is a use-after-free in the SpiderMonkey JavaScript engine's cross-compartment wrapper (CCW) machinery, specifically around Debugger objects. A prior change (bug 1999464) made NukeCrossCompartmentWrappers() skip nuking existing CCWs that target a Debugger instance object, to preserve the link between a Breakpoint and its owning Debugger across realms/compartments (they live in two linked lists in different realms and must stay connected for cleanup). However, the corresponding gatekeeper function AllowNewWrapper(), which decides whether new CCWs may still be created into a realm/compartment whose outgoing/incoming wrappers were already nuked, was not updated with the same exception. This asymmetry breaks an invariant relied upon by Compartment::wrap(): a live CCW to a Debugger object can exist, yet attempting to create a new CCW to that same debugger realm afterward is refused, producing an inconsistent wrapper map state that can be leveraged to use freed/invalid objects (use-after-free) via typical Debugger + nukeAllCCWs()/recomputeWrappers()/gc() usage patterns. Root cause: An earlier fix (bug 1999464) special-cased NukeCrossCompartmentWrappers() to leave CCWs pointing at DebuggerInstanceObject un-nuked, but the matching AllowNewWrapper() gate (which blocks creation of new CCWs into compartments/realms already marked as nuked) was not given the same exception. This mismatch between 'existing wrapper survives' and 'new wrapper creation is still blocked' violates invariants assumed by Compartment::wrap(), leading to corrupted/incoherent wrapper state and eventually use-after-free.
commit_message:
Bug 1999464 - Don't nuke CCWs to the debugger object r=jandem

This is an alternative to the fix in bug 1995637 and removes that change.

The debugger mostly uses its own wrappers for cross compartment pointers
between debugger and debuggee globals. These are not in the CCW map and so are
not nuked by NukeCrossCompartmentWrappers. This pointer from a Breakpoint to
its owning debugger however is a normal CCW that is in the map and so can be
affected by that operation.

The change makes it so we skip nuking CCWs to the main debugger object. This
could affect other uses of this CCW but these are not accessible from content
JS so I don't think this is a problem.

It's important not to break the link between breakpoints and their debuggers
because they are present in two linked lists which are in different realms. To
clean up properly the link needs to be intact.

This change is also covered by the original test in bug 1995637.

findings.message: NukeCrossCompartmentWrappers() was changed so that it skips nuking existing cross-compartment wrappers (CCWs) that point at a Debugger instance object (used to link Breakpoints back to their owning Debugger across realms). However, the companion function js::AllowNewWrapper(), which governs whether a *new* CCW may be created into a compartment/realm that has already had NukeCrossCompartmentWrappers() called on it (via the nukedOutgoingWrappers / nukedIncomingWrappers flags), was left unmodified. This created an inconsistency: an existing CCW to a Debugger instance survives nuking and stays live and usable, but if code subsequently needs to create a *new* CCW to that same (already-nuked) debugger realm -- e.g. while wrapping a fresh reference to the debugger object during debugger operations such as accessing an environment/variable after nukeAllCCWs() -- AllowNewWrapper() unconditionally refuses, since it has no exception for DebuggerInstanceObject. Compartment::wrap() then falls back to producing a dead-object-proxy substitute in a situation where its invariants assume a live wrapper is obtainable (because a live debugger CCW already exists elsewhere), corrupting the compartment's wrapper map: the same debugger object ends up simultaneously represented by a live wrapper and treated through paths that expect a dead one. This mismatched/incoherent wrapper state can be exploited to reach and use a JS object after the compartment's outgoing wrappers were logically invalidated, resulting in a use-after-free (CVE-2026-0884), reproduced by jit-test bug-2003588.js and bug-2003809.js (Debugger + nukeAllCCWs()/recomputeWrappers()/gc() sequences).
findings.suggestion: When introducing an exception in NukeCrossCompartmentWrappers() that leaves an object's existing CCW un-nuked, add the matching exception in AllowNewWrapper() so that new wrappers for the same class of objects (DebuggerInstanceObject) can still be created into a target that has already been marked as nuked. Otherwise the nuke/allow-creation policy diverges and Compartment::wrap()'s invariant that a live wrapper is always obtainable for such objects is violated, leading to wrapper-map corruption and use-after-free.

agent_reasoning: Without this change, the shape/iterator cache can hand out the same NativeIterator to both a full (for-in style) enumeration and an Object.keys scalar-replacement enumeration. An Object.keys iterator built via the "unregistered" fast path only skips enumerator registration for GC/mutation invalidation bookkeeping — it did not otherwise restrict itself to own properties, and nothing stopped a full-enumeration iterator (whose keys may be able to include properties surfaced through a prototype, including a Proxy's own-keys trap) from being reused by the Object.keys path or vice versa. Since OptimizeIteratorIndices/LoadIteratorElement in Ion treat these iterators' cached indices as stable, direct, indexed slot accesses, an attacker could place a Proxy on the prototype chain whose trap runs arbitrary script during enumeration/reuse, invalidating the shapes/slots the JIT assumed were still valid and leading to out-of-bounds or type-confused access. Tagging Object.keys iterators as own-properties-only (via JSITER_OWNONLY and the new OwnPropertiesOnly/NotReusable flag) and refusing to let the two iterator flavors alias each other closes this gap: Object.keys iterators can never gain prototype-chain-derived entries, and a full iterator can never be mistaken for one eligible for the indices fast path's own-property-only guarantee.

findings.message: This newly added LoadIteratorElement branch lets Object.keys iteration use the iterator-indices optimization. For property loads it emits an indexed slot access based on the iterator's cached indices. The earlier iterator cache path can still enumerate/reuse prototype properties, including a Proxy trap that runs script. The reporter's debug-shell input trips the restricted JIT arbitrary-code assertion; a maintainer explains how a mutating trap can invalidate a reused array bounds check.

related_locations.description: Existing cache lookup and iterator reuse without an own-only distinction

findings.suggestion: Use own-properties-only iterators for Object.keys and prevent reuse across enumeration scopes; do not apply the indexed fast path across Proxy side effects.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 670eb2adbc70 on top of intro 3b5eb00effeb via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (UseAfterFree): js::atomics_notify_impl() implements Atomics.notify(). When it discovers that a waiting Atomics.waitAsync() promise was created on the exact same JSContext as the notifying call (a 'same-thread' notification fast path introduced to avoid dispatching an off-thread task to the event loop), it extracts the PromiseObject and defers resolving it until after the futex/helper-thread locks are released, then calls PromiseObject::resolve(cx, promise, resultMsg) directly in a loop. This loop never enters the promise's realm via AutoRealm before resolving it, even though the promise may belong to a different realm than whatever realm happens to be current on cx (a single JSContext can traverse many realms over its lifetime). Resolving a promise while the wrong realm is entered on the context is a known-dangerous pattern in SpiderMonkey and was fixed by adding an AutoRealm scoped to each promise before calling PromiseObject::resolve. Root cause: The same-thread fast path for Atomics.waitAsync()/Atomics.notify() was added without accounting for the fact that JSContext::realm() can differ from the realm of the promise being resolved; the code assumed 'same context' implied 'same realm', which is not guaranteed in a multi-realm embedding like the browser (e.g. cross-origin iframes, Xray wrappers, or other realm-switching operations happening on the same context).

commit_message:
Bug 1467846: Part 20: Don't dispatch task for same-thread notification. r=arai,rhunt

Differential Revision: https://phabricator.services.mozilla.com/D241445

findings.message: In js::atomics_notify_impl, when Atomics.notify() detects that the async waiter it is about to resolve was created by the *same* JSContext (waiter->cx() == cx), it takes a fast path: instead of dispatching an off-thread task to the event loop, it extracts the PromiseObject directly into a `promisesToResolve` vector and later calls PromiseObject::resolve(cx, promisesToResolve[i], resultMsg) on it after leaving the futex/helper-thread lock critical section. However, this resolve loop does not enter the promise's own realm/compartment before calling PromiseObject::resolve. A single JSContext can have multiple realms active over its lifetime (e.g. via cross-realm calls, iframes, Xrays, or realm switches performed by embedders/DevTools), so the promise created by Atomics.waitAsync() may live in a different realm than the one that happens to be current on `cx` at the time atomics_notify_impl() runs the resolve loop. Resolving/reacting to a promise while the wrong realm is entered on the context causes JS::Compartment/Realm-scoped state (i.e. currently-entered global, associated wrappers, GC arena bookkeeping tied to the compartment, and the promise reaction job queueing) to be manipulated inconsistently with the object's actual realm. This class of realm/compartment-mismatch bug in SpiderMonkey has previously led to use-after-free and type-confusion conditions because zone/compartment sweeping and off-thread promise machinery assume the context's current realm matches the object being manipulated.
findings.suggestion: Before resolving each promise in the same-thread fast path, enter the promise's own realm with AutoRealm so that PromiseObject::resolve and the subsequent promise-reaction machinery operate consistently with the object's actual realm/compartment, matching the general convention used elsewhere in SpiderMonkey when manipulating cross-realm objects.
findings.title: Missing AutoRealm when resolving same-thread Atomics.waitAsync promise across realms

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 05ffcde977df on top of intro fcc2f20e35ec via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (UseAfterFree): A one-character bitwise-operator typo in WasmArrayObject::obj_moved() (js/src/wasm/WasmGcObject.cpp) causes the forwarding pointer written for a relocated out-of-line (OOL) WasmGC array data block to always be zero, instead of the new block's address with its low bit set. This corrupted forwarding word is indistinguishable from an inline-array data header, causing Instance::updateFrameForMovingGC() to skip updating wasm-stack-cached data pointers that refer to the relocated OOL block. Wasm code resumes with a stale pointer into freed/reclaimed nursery memory, yielding a use-after-free reachable from web content through WasmGC (shipped enabled by default since Firefox 120). Root cause: In the OOL-forwarding branch of WasmArrayObject::obj_moved(), the intended bitwise-OR operation (`uintptr_t(oolHeaderNew) | 1`) that sets bit 0 of the forwarding pointer while preserving the pointer's upper bits was mistakenly written as a bitwise-AND (`uintptr_t(oolHeaderNew) & 1`). Since OOL header pointers are always aligned (bit 0 naturally clear), the AND operation always yields 0, destroying the forwarding pointer entirely instead of merely setting its tag bit.
commit_message:
Bug 1992888 - Remove the data header from wasm GC inline array allocations.  r=rhunt,bvisness.

This patch reworks WasmArrayObject layout so as to remove the need for a
payload header word in inline allocations.  OOL payloads still need a header
word.  The scheme is:

* IL arrays have no header word.  Instead the payload begins *immediately*
  (with no alignment gap) after the data pointer field.  Because the payload
  array is constrained to be 8-aligned within the object, this means the data
  pointer will hold an 8-aligned value.

* OOL arrays have an 8-byte header, WasmArrayObject::OOLDataHeader header
  word.  Forwarding addresses are stored in OOLDataHeader::word.  In principle
  this can be any value so long as its least significant bit is not zero.
  Hence it is possible to distinguish an IL from OOL payload pointer by
  looking at the word that precedes the pointer; if its least significant bit
  is zero the payload is IL, else it's OOL.

In practice, the OOLDataHeader::word values are used to store forwarding
pointers for the BufferAlloc-managed OOL blocks during GC.  We manage the
reading/writing of the forwarding pointers ourselves, to set their lowest bit
to 1 when storing them, so as to mark the associated area as OOL (see
WasmArrayObject::obj_moved).

When OOL areas are initially created, their header word is set to
OOLDataHeader_Magic, which is suitably misaligned, and is not a valid pointer.

Hence it is possible to also tell whether an OOL area has ever been relocated,
since relocation will overwrite the initial OOLDataHeader_Magic value.

The patch tightens up, and documents, the WasmArrayObject layout.  This is
necessary in order to guarantee that (1) the IL data area has an offset that is
0 % 8, and (2) that the `data_` field is right at the end of the object.

Main changes:

* WasmArrayObject::obj_moved, WasmStructObject::obj_moved: changes to store
  the forwarding address of an OOL block in the old block's
  OOLDataHeader::word field.

* Instance::updateFrameForMovingGC: update array OOL pointers using the
  forwarding addresses stored by WasmArrayObject::obj_moved.

* class WasmArrayObject: rework; tighten up layout a lot; add static assertions
  accordingly; simplify methods relating to layout/offsets.

* terminology: change `storageBytes` to `arrayDataBytes`.
