 //=========================================================================
 // WasmArrayObject
 
-// Class for a wasm array. It contains a pointer to the array contents and
-// possibly inline data. Array data is allocated with a DataHeader that tracks
-// whether the array data is stored inline in a trailing array, or out of line
-// in heap memory. The array's data pointer will always point at the start of
-// the array data, and the data header can always be read by subtracting
-// sizeof(DataHeader).
+// [SMDOC] WasmArrayObject layout
+//
+// `class WasmArrayObject` represents wasm-GC arrays in the JS heap.
+//
+// For zero-sized and small arrays, which are common, the data is stored
+// in-line (IL) immediately after the end of the WasmArrayObject.
+//
+// For arrays too large to represent IL, the WasmArrayObject points to an
+// out-of-line (OOL) storage area that is managed by js::gc::BufferAllocator,
+// which holds all of the elements.  This OOL area is sometimes referred to
+// below as the "OOL block"; note however it consists of a one-word
+// OOLDataHeader followed by the actual array data.
+//
+// Layout of WasmArrayObjects and their associated OOL areas is constrained by
+// multiple requirements:
+//
+// (1) There must be a pointer to the storage array (the "array data pointer"
+//     or just "data pointer"), that can be used as a base for indexing without
+//     regard to whether the data is IL or OOL.
+//
+// (2) The array data areas must be 8-aligned, even on 32-bit targets, so that
+//     int64/double accesses are aligned.
+//
+// (3) The layout must offer a way to update on-stack data pointers on minor
+//     collections, without having access to the parent object.
+//
+// (4) The layout must be as compact as reasonably possible.
+//
+// (5) The IL array data must begin immediately after the end of the preceding
+//     field (`data*`), with no alignment hole in between.  This is critical;
+//     the scheme won't work without this.
+//
+// (6) [Derived from 2 and 5] The size of WasmArrayObject must be 0 % 8.
+//
+// (7) [Derived from 2] The size of WasmArrayObject::OOLDataHeader
+//     must be 0 % 8.
+//
+// (8) [Derived from 5] offsetof(WasmArrayObject, data_) + sizeof(data_)
+//                      == sizeof(WasmArrayObject).
+//
+// (9) It is assumed that the underlying JSObject and BufferAlloc allocators
+//     produce memory that is at least 0 % 8.  Without that, all of the above
+//     is pointless.
+//
+// The layout complexity starts at the data* field.  Adding extra fields before
+// the data* field should have no effect, so long as the added field(s) have a
+// size which is a multiple of 8 bytes.
+//
+// -------- 64-bit targets --------
+//
+// Layout is as follows:
+//
+// * Each `| name |` unit is an 8-aligned, 8-byte word,
+//   except for the `| ..arrayData.. |` fields, which are 8-aligned and
+//   a multiple of 8 bytes long (including zero).
+//
+// * "padding / #elems" means the 32-bit `numElements_` field and the 4 bytes
+//   padding that precedes it.
+//
+// : 0    7 : 8    15 : 16   23  24  31 : 32    // byte offset
+// : JS     : WasmGc  : WasmArray       :       // class name
+// : Object : Object  : Object          :
+// :        :         :                 :
+// |        | Super   | padding |       |               |        (IL case)
+// | Shape* | TypeVec |  #elems | data* | ..arrayData.. |
+//                                 | |    |
+//                                 | \-->-/
+//                                 |
+//                                 | | header | ..arrayData.. |  (OOL case)
+//                                 |            |
+//                                 \--->---->---/
+//
+// For the IL case, the array data area starts at offset 32, so is 8-aligned.
+// The OOL allocation as a whole is 8-aligned, and the header is 1 word long,
+// so the array data is also 8-aligned.
+//
+// -------- 32-bit targets --------
+//
+// Layout is as follows:
+//
+// * Each `| name |` unit is an 4-aligned, 4-byte word,
+//   except for the `| ..arrayData.. |` fields, which have the same
+//   constraints as the 64-bit layout: 8-aligned and
+//   a multiple of 8 bytes long (including zero).
+//
+// * Both `padd/ing` fields are 4 bytes long.
+//
+// : 0    3   4  7 : 8    11 : 12 15  16  19   20 23 : 24  // byte offset
+// : JS            : WasmGc  : WasmArray             :     // class name
+// : Object        : Object  : Object                :
+// :               :         :                       :
+// |        | padd | Super   | padd |        |       |               |
+// | Shape* |  ing | TypeVec |  ing | #elems | data* | ..arrayData.. |
+//                                              | |    |         (IL case)
+//                                              v \-->-/
+//                                              |
+//                         | padding | header | ..arrayData.. |  (OOL case)
+//
+// For the IL case, the array data area starts at offset 24, so is 8-aligned.
+// The OOL block as a whole is 8-aligned, and the header word and padding
+// together are 8 bytes, so the array data is also 8-aligned.
+//
+// Note 1: Don't confuse JSObject::padding (not discussed further),
+//         WasmArrayObject::padding (discussed here) and
+//         OOLDataHeader::padding (see below).  These are unrelated.
+//
+// Note 2: WasmArrayObject::padding is omitted on 32-bit Windows.  On that
+//         platform, it appears that JSObject occupies offsets 0 .. 7 inclusive
+//         (as shown), but WasmGcObject occupies offsets 8 .. 15 inclusive
+//         (*not* as shown), which then causes the array data to start at
+//         offset 28, not 24.  The reason for this is unknown.  It may be to do
+//         with incomplete empty-base-class optimization in MSVC and clang-cl,
+//         given that `TrailingArray` is an empty class.  However, adding
+//         MOZ_EMPTY_BASES does not help.
+//
+//         The manual fix -- removal of the `padding` field -- restores the
+//         positioning of #elems, data* and payload.
+//
+// -------- OOL Header words --------
+//
+// The OOL header word (OOLDataHeader::word) is used both for block forwarding
+// and to know whether a data pointer is IL or OOL, without having access to
+// its parent WasmArrayObject.
+//
+// This is done by looking at the word immediately preceding what the data
+// pointer points at.  There are 3 possible cases:
+//
+// (a) The data is IL, so the word preceding what the data pointer points at is
+//     the data* pointer itself (WasmArrayObject::data_).  From (2) above we
+//     know this is 8-aligned, so the value stored there ends in 0b000.
+//
+// (b) The data is OOL and the header word holds a forwarding address.  We
+//     manage forwarding addresses ourselves, and so set bit 0 to 1 to indicate
+//     it's a forwarding address.
+//
+// (c) The data is OOL but has never been forwarded.  The header word will have
+//     been initialized to OOLDataHeader_Magic, a constant that has bit 0 set
+//     to 1, and, even if the bit 0 was zero, would never be a feasible
+//     pointer.
+//
+// Hence, given a data pointer, we can determine whether the data is IL or OOL
+// thusly:
+//
+//   data-is-IL  =  (((uintptr_t*)data_pointer)[-1] & 1) == 0
+//
+// If the data isn't IL, then ((uintptr_t*)data_pointer)[-1] either holds a
+// forwarding pointer or not, thus:
+//
+//   has_forwarding_pointer
+//     = !block-is-IL && ((uintptr_t*)data_pointer)[-1] != OOLDataHeader_Magic
+//
+// -------- Other comments --------
+//
+// Throughout the implementation, a value with name `arrayDataBytes` holds the
+// size, in bytes, of a `| ..arrayData.. |` area.  It is exactly the number of
+// bytes required to hold the stored elements.  Hence, if the data area is OOL,
+// the size of the (BufferAllocator-managed) block is `arrayDataBytes +
+// sizeof(OOLDataHeader)`, that is, `arrayDataBytes + 8`.
+//
+// -------- end --------
+

intro_commit_message:
Bug 1992888 - Remove the data header from wasm GC inline array allocations.  r=rhunt,bvisness.

This patch reworks WasmArrayObject layout so as to remove the need for a
payload header word in inline allocations.  OOL payloads still need a header
word.  The scheme is:

* IL arrays have no header word.  Instead the payload begins *immediately*
  (with no alignment gap) after the data pointer field.  Because the payload
  array is constrained to be 8-aligned within the object, this means the data
  pointer will hold an 8-aligned value.

* OOL arrays have an 8-byte header, WasmArrayObject::OOLDataHeader header
  word.  Forwarding addresses are stored in OOLDataHeader::word.  In principle
  this can be any value so long as its least significant bit is not zero.
  Hence it is possible to distinguish an IL from OOL payload pointer by
  looking at the word that precedes the pointer; if its least significant bit
  is zero the payload is IL, else it's OOL.

In practice, the OOLDataHeader::word values are used to store forwarding
pointers for the BufferAlloc-managed OOL blocks during GC.  We manage the
reading/writing of the forwarding pointers ourselves, to set their lowest bit
to 1 when storing them, so as to mark the associated area as OOL (see
WasmArrayObject::obj_moved).

When OOL areas are initially created, their header word is set to
OOLDataHeader_Magic, which is suitably misaligned, and is not a valid pointer.

Hence it is possible to also tell whether an OOL area has ever been relocated,
since relocation will overwrite the initial OOLDataHeader_Magic value.

The patch tightens up, and documents, the WasmArrayObject layout.  This is
necessary in order to guarantee that (1) the IL data area has an offset that is
0 % 8, and (2) that the `data_` field is right at the end of the object.

Main changes:

* WasmArrayObject::obj_moved, WasmStructObject::obj_moved: changes to store
  the forwarding address of an OOL block in the old block's
  OOLDataHeader::word field.

* Instance::updateFrameForMovingGC: update array OOL pointers using the
  forwarding addresses stored by WasmArrayObject::obj_moved.

* class WasmArrayObject: rework; tighten up layout a lot; add static assertions
  accordingly; simplify methods relating to layout/offsets.

* terminology: change `storageBytes` to `arrayDataBytes`.

findings.message: When a WasmArrayObject with out-of-line (OOL) array data is promoted/relocated during a nursery minor GC, obj_moved() is supposed to store a forwarding pointer to the new OOL block location in the old block's OOLDataHeader::word field, with bit 0 set to mark it as a valid forwarding pointer (this bit is the documented protocol used by isDataInline()/Instance::updateFrameForMovingGC() to distinguish OOL forwarding words from inline array data). The code instead computes `uintptr_t(oolHeaderNew) & 1`, a bitwise AND, rather than `uintptr_t(oolHeaderNew) | 1`, a bitwise OR. Because oolHeaderNew is always an aligned pointer (its low bits are zero), the AND expression evaluates to 0 for every invocation, discarding the entire forwarding pointer and producing a header word indistinguishable from an inline-array header word (whose bit 0 is also clear). Consequently, Instance::updateFrameForMovingGC(), which reads this word via WasmArrayObject::isDataInline() to decide whether a wasm-stack-cached ArrayDataPointer needs to be redirected to the array's new location, misclassifies the moved OOL data as inline. It takes the inline code path, computes a bogus WasmArrayObject* from the stale data pointer, finds (via MaybeForwarded) that the bogus pointer is unchanged, and therefore leaves the stack slot pointing at the old (now freed/reused) nursery memory. Wasm code that resumes execution after the GC then reads and potentially writes through this stale pointer, resulting in a use-after-free that is reachable from untrusted web content via WasmGC (array.new/array.get/array.set across a call that can trigger a minor GC).
findings.suggestion: Use bitwise OR instead of AND so the forwarding pointer's value is preserved while its low bit is forced to 1 (the documented OOL marker), e.g. add an assertion that the pointer is already aligned (bit 0 clear) before OR-ing in the marker bit, matching the eventual upstream fix.
findings.suggestion_code:
MOZ_ASSERT((uintptr_t(oolHeaderNew) & 1) == 0);
oolHeaderOld->word = uintptr_t(oolHeaderNew) | 1;

ground_truth.root_cause: In the OOL-forwarding branch of WasmArrayObject::obj_moved(), the intended bitwise-OR operation (`uintptr_t(oolHeaderNew) | 1`) that sets bit 0 of the forwarding pointer while preserving the pointer's upper bits was mistakenly written as a bitwise-AND (`uintptr_t(oolHeaderNew) & 1`). Since OOL header pointers are always aligned (bit 0 naturally clear), the AND operation always yields 0, destroying the forwarding pointer entirely instead of merely setting its tag bit.

pr_description:
This patch reworks WasmArrayObject layout so as to remove the need for a
payload header word in inline allocations.  OOL payloads still need a header
word.  The scheme is:

* IL arrays have no header word.  Instead the payload begins *immediately*
  (with no alignment gap) after the data pointer field.  Because the payload
  array is constrained to be 8-aligned within the object, this means the data
  pointer will hold an 8-aligned value.

* OOL arrays have an 8-byte header, WasmArrayObject::OOLDataHeader header
  word.  Forwarding addresses are stored in OOLDataHeader::word.  In principle
  this can be any value so long as its least significant bit is not zero.
  Hence it is possible to distinguish an IL from OOL payload pointer by
  looking at the word that precedes the pointer; if its least significant bit
  is zero the payload is IL, else it's OOL.

In practice, the OOLDataHeader::word values are used to store forwarding
pointers for the BufferAlloc-managed OOL blocks during GC.  We manage the
reading/writing of the forwarding pointers ourselves, to set their lowest bit
to 1 when storing them, so as to mark the associated area as OOL (see
WasmArrayObject::obj_moved).

When OOL areas are initially created, their header word is set to
OOLDataHeader_Magic, which is suitably misaligned, and is not a valid pointer.

Hence it is possible to also tell whether an OOL area has ever been relocated,
since relocation will overwrite the initial OOLDataHeader_Magic value.

The patch tightens up, and documents, the WasmArrayObject layout.  This is
necessary in order to guarantee that (1) the IL data area has an offset that is
0 % 8, and (2) that the `data_` field is right at the end of the object.

Main changes:

* WasmArrayObject::obj_moved, WasmStructObject::obj_moved: changes to store
  the forwarding address of an OOL block in the old block's
  OOLDataHeader::word field.

* Instance::updateFrameForMovingGC: update array OOL pointers using the
  forwarding addresses stored by WasmArrayObject::obj_moved.

* class WasmArrayObject: rework; tighten up layout a lot; add static assertions
  accordingly; simplify methods relating to layout/offsets.

* terminology: change `storageBytes` to `arrayDataBytes`.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix e055cf04d23f on top of intro 398a31295dff via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (UseAfterFree): After migrating BaseScript's PrivateScriptData storage to use the GC BufferAllocator (Bug 2002790), BaseScript::swapData() continued to rely solely on GCStructPtr::set()'s write barrier, which only barriers the GC things referenced from within PrivateScriptData, not the buffer allocation pointer (data_) itself. Since the buffer allocation can now live in the nursery and be moved/freed independently, failing to barrier the data_ edge itself can cause the GC to lose track of (or prematurely free) the old PrivateScriptData buffer during script delazification/relazification, leading to a later use-after-free style access when the tracer walks a stale buffer pointer, producing an assertion failure (`isAllocated(alloc)`) or SEGV inside BufferAllocator code. Root cause: BaseScript::swapData/releaseData assumed that GCStructPtr::set() barriers were sufficient for updating the data_ pointer, which was true when PrivateScriptData was a plain heap allocation. Once Bug 2002790 made data_ a BufferAllocator-managed (nursery-capable) allocation, the pointer itself became a GC edge requiring its own trace/write barrier (via TraceBufferEdge), which was not added at the same time, leaving a gap between allocation-strategy change and barrier coverage.

findings.message: BaseScript::swapData() updates the BaseScript::data_ pointer (a BufferAllocator-managed allocation holding PrivateScriptData) using only `data_.set(zone(), other)`. That GCStructPtr::set() call only triggers a write barrier for the *contents* pointed to by data_ (i.e. the GC things referenced from inside PrivateScriptData), but it performs no write/read barrier for the buffer allocation pointer itself. Before Bug 2002790, PrivateScriptData was a plain malloc'd UniquePtr-owned buffer with no GC-tracing concerns of its own, so this was fine. After Bug 2002790 migrated PrivateScriptData to be allocated via the nursery-aware BufferAllocator (gc::NewSizedBuffer), the data_ pointer itself became a GC-managed edge that can point into the nursery and needs to be traced/barriered like any other GC edge (via TraceBufferEdge), not just the GC things nested within it. Because swapData() replaces data_ without first tracing/barriering the old buffer pointer, an incremental or generational GC can lose track of the old nursery-allocated buffer when a script is delazified/relazified (e.g. swapData is invoked from createPrivateScriptData/fullyInitFromStencil/relazify). This leads to a stale/dangling buffer pointer later being traced as if it were a valid BufferAllocator allocation, producing a SEGV / `isAllocated(alloc)` assertion failure in BufferAllocatorInternals.h when the tracer (js::PrivateScriptData::trace -> TraceManuallyBarrieredGCCellPtr -> BufferAllocator::isNurseryOwned/traceEdge) accesses the corrupted/freed allocation -- effectively a use-after-free of the buffer allocation metadata.
findings.suggestion: Before overwriting data_ with the new buffer in swapData (and before clearing it in releaseData/freeData), explicitly trace/barrier the old buffer allocation pointer itself (not just its GC-thing contents) using TraceBufferEdge when the zone needs a marking barrier, mirroring the fix: check `if (data_ && zone()->needsMarkingBarrier())` and call `TraceBufferEdge(zone()->barrierTracer(), this, &data_, "BaseScript::swapData barrier")` prior to `data_.set(zone(), other)`. More generally, provide a GCStructPtr/edge abstraction that barriers both the buffer-allocation pointer and its contents uniformly so future buffer-allocator migrations don't reintroduce this class of bug.
